newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. body says mail will grow despite Internet.
newsitem.headline: U.N. body says mail will grow despite Internet.

text.p: The volume of letters sent through the traditional post around the world is expected to grow by up to five per cent to the year 2005 despite the challenge from electronic (e-)mail, a U.N. report said on Tuesday.
But the report, compiled by the Berne-based Universal Postal Union (UPU), said the share of physical mail would drop from 20 to less than 15 per cent of the surging overall communications market.
E-mail would double its share from five to 10 per cent, while telephone and facsimile (fax) would remain static at around 75 per cent.

The United Nations agency said the findings were based on figures and estimates from 90 national postal administrations around the world and on statistics on trends in mail services it had compiled for many years.

UPU Director-General Thomas Leavey said the survey showed "that all current providers of postal services, whether they enjoy monopoly protection or not, will have to face a future environment quite different from the current situation".
The survey said the communications market as a whole was progressing much faster than the postal market.

But while in most countries the entire population had access to postal services, availability of telephone and fax was still restricted and in many regions of the world development of e-mail was very limited.

According to the UPU, 403 billion letters were handled in 1995 by more than six million postal employees around the globe. Of these, 98 per cent were domestic mail remaining within the country where they were posted.
The study said domestic letter traffic was likely to increase by 2.5 per cent a year until the year 2005, well ahead of the just under one per cent recorded globally between 1985 and 1995.

The advance would be underpinned by strong growth in use of traditional mail in emerging economies and developing countries, as growth in richer nations was expected to slow from 2.7 per cent to an average of 2.3 per cent.

International mail traffic was set to grow in volume between 1995 and 2005 at a rate of 3.4 to 5.2 per cent, depending on the region. The highest growth was expected in lower income countries, according to the UPU.
The report said the greatest effect of the development of e-mail would be in business, where by the year 2005 more than 50 per cent of firms would be able to use it.
But in a comment on the findings, Leavey said fax and e-mail also generated more physical mail.
